Reynolds, University of Melbourne, Melbourne, Australia #### **Funding information** ACT government #### **Abstract** Organizations and their leaders are recognized as key players in staff well-being and engagement but there is limited longitudinal research with large samples. Moreover, it is not clear how specifically leader behaviour impacts on wellbeing. Based on the social identity approach, we argue that school leaders who are capable of crafting and clarifying what it means to be an organizational member while actively representing the groups' interests—an identity leader—will be able to foster a positive school climate. In turn, this positive climate should result in a range of positive outcomes for school staff members, including better well-being and engagement in their work. Using a longitudinal survey of over 6000 school staff, we found support for our hypothesis: school staff members who perceived their school leaders as being identity leaders perceived a more positive school climate 1 year later, which, in turn, predicted higher levels of well-being (lower burnout, lower stress and higher self-esteem) and engagement in school outcomes (higher organizational commitment, team morale and professional development). Overall, these results underline the key role that school identity leaders play in crafting positive working environments and outcomes for staff members. #### **KEYWORDS** burnout, engagement, identity leadership, leadership, organizational climate, school climate, well-being This is an open access article under the terms of the [Creative Commons Attribution](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited. © 2024 The Authors. *Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psycholog y* published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd on behalf of The British Psychological Society. The well-being of staff is paramount to organizational performance and success. This is particularly so in educational contexts where poor experiences of school staff directly relate to reduced student performance. For example, emotional exhaustion in school staff is associated with worse students' school grades, standardized achievement test scores and school satisfaction (Arens & Morin, [2016\)](#page-21-0). Similarly, school staff engagement at work is pivotal. A workforce that is highly engaged will be committed towards the goals and mission of schools, showing better performance and team morale (e.g., Bakker et al., [2008\)](#page-21-1). Thus, schools that invest in fostering their employees' well-being and engagement can see significant improvements in staff, and subsequently in schools and the quality of education. One key factor contributing to employee well-being and engagement is effective leadership (Robertson & Flint-Taylor, [2008](#page-23-0)). While emerging syntheses demonstrate a consistent association between leadership and employees' well-being (Kuoppala et al., [2008](#page-23-1)) and engagement (Decuypere & Schaufeli, [2021](#page-22-0)), most of the work has focused on the *dyadic relation between leaders and followers*, particularly from a transformational leadership perspective (e.g., Arnold, [2017](#page-21-2); Harms et al., [2017](#page-22-1); Kuoppala et al., [2008\)](#page-23-1). In the current study, we answer the call to go beyond dyadic conceptualizations of leadership (Harms et al., [2017](#page-22-1)) and approach leadership from a *group-based* perspective (identity leadership; Epitropaki et al., [2017;](#page-22-2) Haslam et al., [2020\)](#page-22-3). From this framework, good leadership—and its positive influence on followers' well-being and engagement—is a direct consequence of recognizing and harnessing the power of being a model group member of one's organzation, of being one of 'us' and doing things for 'our' interest (e.g., Steffens, Haslam, Kerschreiter, Schuh, & van Dick, [2014;](#page-24-0) Steffens, Haslam, & Reicher, [2014](#page-24-1)). However, its potential impact in schools remains untested. Moreover, while growing evidence suggests that identity leadership promotes better employee outcomes, little is known about *how* identity leaders can foster these outcomes. Our study examines whether school identity leaders can create a positive *organizational* (*or school*) *climate* that promotes better well-being and engagement in staff members using a 3-year longitudinal design and a broad range of well-being (burnout disengagement, burnout exhaustion, stress and self-esteem) and engagement measures (organizational commitment, professional development and team morale). Thus, our research is well positioned to examine the broad and long-term consequences of identity leadership along with its mechanism of influence, with direct implications for the way schools and other organizations shape their future leaders. # **Leadership and its impact on followers** Leadership and its potential impact on followers' engagement and well-being has received significant empirical attention. Leaders' behaviours—such as their fairness, and support—is associated with staff members' well-being (Dyrbye et al., [2021;](#page-22-4) Perko et al., [2016;](#page-23-2) van Dierendonck et al., [2004](#page-25-0); Winkler et al., [2015](#page-25-1)) and better performance (student performance; Heck & Hallinger, [2010](#page-22-5); team performance; Keller, [2006\)](#page-23-3) *later in time*. In recent years, systematic reviews and meta-analyses have emerged with the goal of integrating what is known about leadership, well-being and staff engagement. Kuoppala et al. [\(2008\)](#page-23-1) found a positive association between leadership and well-being (but not engagement) in a review of 109 studies. Similarly, in their meta-analysis on the effect of leadership on staff's mental health (including 144 articles), Montano et al. [\(2017\)](#page-23-4) found a positive association between leadership and their followers' mental health. Another meta-analyses of 157 independent samples by Harms et al. ([2017](#page-22-1)) found that transformational leadership and leader-member exchange (LMX) were associated with less burnout and stress, while an abusive style of supervision was associated with these negative outcomes (see also Arnold, [2017\)](#page-21-2). In terms of engagement, meta-analyses have found that transformational leadership is associated with better individual performance (Wang et al., [2011\)](#page-25-2), while LMX leadership is associated with more commitment and lower turnover intentions of staff (Gerstner & Day, [1997](#page-22-6)). In contrast, destructive forms of leadership are negatively associated with staff engagement (individual performance, commitment and turnover intentions; Schyns & Schilling, [2013\)](#page-24-2). Importantly, these reviews also highlight several limitations in existing research. First, while much of the previous research has focused on transformational and dyadic forms of leadership (e.g., Arnold, [2017](#page-21-2)), SCHOOL IDENTITY LEADERSHIP **| 3** group-based leadership—one in which school leaders recognize and strengthen their position as *group members* (Haslam et al., [2021;](#page-22-7) Hogg, [2001;](#page-22-8) Thomas et al., [2013](#page-24-3)) is quickly gaining interest for its potential to improve organizational performance. This group-form of leadership focuses on leaders as being *part* of a group, as opposed to being *apart* from the group due to their unique characteristics (being transformational or instructional). Second, the *process* explaining how group-based leadership impacts staff requires further investigation. Third, the great majority of the previous research is cross-sectional. In their metaanalysis, Montano et al. ([2017](#page-23-4)) conclude that one of the deficiencies in this area of research is 'a paucity of longitudinal studies' (p. 344; see also Arnold, [2017\)](#page-21-2), and hence it is unclear whether the influence of leadership could be observed in time. Our research aims to address each of these limitations. # **Identity leadership: A group approach to school leadership** The identity leadership framework was developed to address the group-based nature of leadership, namely that leaders and followers are often part of the same group, and they are subject to group dynamics that influence their relations (Haslam et al., [2021;](#page-22-7) Hirst et al., [2009](#page-22-9); Hogg, [2001\)](#page-22-8). This analysis is based on the social identity approach, which recognizes people's capacity to internalize their group memberships into their self-concept, such that the self is defined by 'we' and 'us' (and not simply 'I' and 'me'; Reicher et al., [2005;](#page-23-5) Tajfel & Turner, [1979;](#page-24-4) Turner et al., [1987](#page-24-5); Turner & Haslam, [2001;](#page-24-6) Turner & Reynolds, [2012](#page-24-7)). Thinking of ourselves as members of a group directly impacts cognition, emotion and behaviour. A plethora of research has demonstrated that we are more likely to be attracted to (Hogg & Hardie, [1991\)](#page-22-10), listen to (Greenaway et al., [2015](#page-22-11)) and trust (Platow et al., [2012](#page-23-6)) members of our group. There is also evidence that groups are essential to well-being and have implications for mortality (Steffens, Cruwys, et al., [2016\)](#page-24-8) and mental health (Haslam et al., [2016](#page-22-12)), including in organizations (Steffens et al., [2017\)](#page-24-9). Thus, group processes have important implications for influence and well-being. For example, in schools, staff for whom being a member of school is central to their self-view (those who identify strongly with their school) experience greater job involvement and self-esteem as well as lower depression (Bizumic et al., [2009](#page-21-3)). The identity leadership model (Haslam et al., [2021](#page-22-7); Hogg, [2001](#page-22-8); Steffens et al., [2018;](#page-24-10) Steffens, Haslam, Kerschreiter, Schuh, & van Dick, [2014;](#page-24-0) Steffens, Haslam, & Reicher, [2014](#page-24-1)) applied the insights gained from the social identity approach to our understanding of leadership. According to this model, the most effective leaders will recognize and harness the power of their shared group membership. As members of the one group, identity leaders can engage in processes of social influence, and in so doing, foster the engagement and well-being of staff members. Moreover, their shared group membership confers them with the characteristics they need to influence followers, including trustworthiness (Giessner & Van Knippenberg, [2008](#page-22-13)) and charisma (Platow et al., [2006](#page-23-7)). In schools—as in organizations more broadly— identity leaders can be characterized by four broad behaviours to influence group members (Steffens, Haslam, & Reicher, [2014\)](#page-24-1). First, school identity leaders would aim at being representatives of their school, embodying the characteristics that define the school (i.e., identity prototypicality). Second, school identity leaders would champion the school and its interests in ways that are consistent with the school's identity (i.e., identity advancement; Haslam et al., [2021](#page-22-7)). Third, school identity leaders would be entrepreneurs of the school's identity, constructing and clarifying the groups' meaning strategically so that the leaders are concrete manifestations of the group (i.e., identity entrepreneurship; Augoustinos & De Garis, [2012\)](#page-21-4). Lastly, school identity leaders would have the capacity to embed the group identity by creating environments and structures in which staff members can live out the vision of the group (i.e., identity impresarioship; Haslam et al., [2021](#page-22-7)). In summary, (school) identity leaders are prototypical group members (one of 'us'), champion the group (do things for 'us'), shape a shared group identity (craft a sense of 'us'), and they embed their vision of the group identity into their actions (make 'us' matter; Haslam et al., [2021;](#page-22-7) Steffens, Haslam, & Reicher, [2014](#page-24-1)). As an emerging—and slowly maturing—area of research, there is increased evidence that identity leadership is related to better well-being and engagement in organizations. A recent meta-analysis revealed that leaders had greater influence (e.g., on role performance and team cohesion) when they were perceived as more prototypical of the group (Steffens et al., [2021\)](#page-24-11). Participants were also more likely to support a political leader when they were perceived as championing the interests of their group (Steffens, Mols, et al., [2016;](#page-24-12) van Knippenberg & van Knippenberg, [2005](#page-25-3)). Perceived identity entrepreneurship was associated with higher engagement and lower burnout in a repeated measures design (Coffeng et al., [2021](#page-22-14)). In a study of 7294 participants across 28 countries and 31 samples (one of which was longitudinal), higher perception of identity leadership was associated with lower burnout (van Dick et al., [2021\)](#page-24-13). In a follow up study, identity leadership was associated with greater innovation above and beyond other forms of leadership (LMX leadership, transformational leadership and authentic leadership; Bracht et al., [2023](#page-22-15)). However, the application of identity leaders to schools, and its potential longitudinal relations (two or more years later), remains to be systematically tested. Thus, the first goal of this research is to test how school identity leadership relates to staff well-being and engagement in a longitudinal model. # **Why identity leaders influence followers: Organizational climate** One critical proposition from identity leadership is that leaders impact the everyday experience of staff at work. One way of doing so is creating a positive and clear *organizational climate*, one in which the members of the organization feel they belong and thrive. Organizational climate refers to the perceptions of the work environment (Rousseau, [1988](#page-23-8)), including the meaning attached to the work environment, reward behaviour, policies, practices and procedures (Rousseau, [1988;](#page-23-8) Schneider et al., [2013](#page-24-14)). These perceptions are shared through interactions with others, becoming meaningful understandings of the group/organization (Schneider et al., [2017\)](#page-24-15). A positive organizational climate is associated with lower turnover intentions (Ryu et al., [2020](#page-23-9)), higher staff knowledge-sharing (Al-Kurdi et al., [2020](#page-21-5)) and higher organizational commitment (Hu et al., [2022](#page-23-10)). Organizational climate is also related to better staff well-being, including lower stress (Loh et al., [2019](#page-23-11)) and lower burn-out later in time (Idris et al., [2014\)](#page-23-12). In the school context, a positive *school climate* (shared values and norms, an academic emphasis that promotes and supports learning, and positive relations; Thapa et al., [2013](#page-24-16)) is associated with better well-being and motivation among staff, including lower burnout rates (Grayson & Alvarez, [2008](#page-22-16)) and higher satisfaction with the job and self-efficacy (Taylor & Tashakkori, [1995\)](#page-24-17). In the broad leadership literature, leaders are expected to play an important role in creating and moulding the organizations' socio-cultural environment. Indeed, there is a dynamic interplay between leaders and the social environments they create and promote (Schein, [1992\)](#page-24-18), as was initially demonstrated by Lewin's classical studies on leadership styles (Lewin et al., [1999/1939\)](#page-23-13). Since the early 2000s, there has been an increased interest in how and when leaders forge positive climates (e.g., Barling et al., [2002](#page-21-6); Cole et al., [2013](#page-22-17)). For example, transformational leadership was associated with better business unit performance partly because it was related to a higher achievement culture in the organization (Xenikou & Simosi, [2006\)](#page-25-4). In school research, leadership is important for a positive school climate (McCarley et al., [2016](#page-23-14)) and associated school identification (Bizumic et al., [2009\)](#page-21-3). Identity leaders are particularly well suited to support a clear, coherent, meaningful and rewarding organizational climate. Given how they champion the group, craft a shared meaning and identity, and embed this meaning in everyday practice (Haslam et al., [2021\)](#page-22-7), identity leaders can effectively create a work environment (i.e., an organizational climate) that facilitates well-being and engagement. This remains to be tested, especially in a school context. # **Current study and hypotheses** The goal of this study was two-fold. First, it tested whether perceiving school leaders to be identity leaders (representatives, crafters, champions and entrepreneurs of the school) impacted on employees' self-reported well-being and engagement. Second, it examined the mechanism by which this process occurs, and more precisely, whether perceived identity leadership fostered a more positive school climate, which in turn facilitated staff wellbeing and organizational engagement. **Hypothesis 2.** Identity leadership in Wave 1 will be associated with higher levels of school climate at Wave 2. In turn, school climate at Wave 2 will be associated with better well-being and organizational engagement Wave 3. We tested these hypotheses using a three-wave longitudinal study, which enabled us to test the temporal association of these relations. Critically, by controlling for initial levels of the mediator and outcome variables, we tested the extent to which initial levels of identity leadership are associated with residuals (or changes) in these variables in time. The hypothesized model is presented in Figure [1](#page-4-0). # **METHOD** # **Participants and procedure** This research was part of an ongoing collaboration between the Australian National University and a government education department in Australia. The project involves staff responses from 89 public schools, who answered the survey during the third term of 2018, 2019 and 2020. This is part of their annual school satisfaction survey. Consent was obtained from all respondents. Respondents who changed schools in the 3 years of the study (*n*=209) were removed from the data given the goal to study the influence of the same leadership and organizational climate across years. The number of participants that answered at least one of the waves was 6373 (*n*Wave 1=3611; *n*Wave 2=3606; *n*Wave 3=4302). In Wave 1, 80% of the sample was working full time (20% part time). For information on sex, years of experience and age categories across waves, see Table [1.](#page-6-0) Only participants who had answered the identity leadership question in 2018 were retained for the main analyses. # **Measures** The items of all the measures we employed can be found in Data [S1](#page-25-5) ([https://osf.io/hyrp5/?view\\_only=](https://osf.io/hyrp5/?view_only=06865fd72c6e4646839fa855d43e8f28) [06865fd72c6e4646839fa855d43e8f28](https://osf.io/hyrp5/?view_only=06865fd72c6e4646839fa855d43e8f28)). Unless otherwise specified, all items used a Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree); for each scale, items were averaged such that higher scores represent a greater presence of the construct. # Identity leadership School identity leadership was measured using 15 items of the identity leadership inventory (Steffens, Haslam, Reicher, Platow, et al., [2014](#page-24-19); Van Dick et al., [2018](#page-24-20), [2021\)](#page-24-13), measuring the four components of identity leadership (identity prototypicality, identity advancement, identity impresarioship, and identity entrepreneurship). An example item is 'the leadership embodies what this school stands for'. The scale had excellent reliability at Wave 1 (*α*=.98). # Organizational or school climate The organizational climate of schools—that is, school climate—was measured with the school climate subscales of the staff school climate and school identification measurement scale (Lee et al., [2017](#page-23-15)) at Waves 1 and 2. This scale assesses school climate with questions such as 'staff are friendly to students'. The scale had excellent reliability at Wave 1 (*α*=.96) and Wave 2 (*α*=.96). # Well-being Stress and self-esteem were measured in Waves 1 and 3, whereas burnout was only assessed in Wave 3. *Stress* was assessed with the stress subscale of the short-form version of the depression anxiety stress scale (DASS-21; Antony et al., [1998](#page-21-7)). This was adapted to measure stress at work by Bizumic et al. ([2009;](#page-21-3) Wave 1: *α*=.91; Wave 3: *α*=.91). Participants indicated how much each statement characterized them using a scale from 0 (Does not apply) to 3 (Very much; e.g., 'I tended to over-react to situations'). *Self-esteem* was measured with a four-item modified version of the Rosenberg Self-esteem Scale (Bizumic et al., [2009](#page-21-3); Rosenberg, [1965\)](#page-23-16). Participants provided their response to items (e.g., 'I take a positive attitude towards myself') using a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree). The scale showed good reliability in Wave 1 (*α*=.80) and Wave 3 (*α*=.78). *Burnout exhaustion and disengagement* were measured in Wave 3 with the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory (Halbesleben & Demerouti, [2005;](#page-22-18) Reis et al., [2015](#page-23-17)) which includes 16 items, eight measuring exhaustion (e.g., 'There are days when I feel tired before I arrive at work') and eight focusing on disengagement (e.g., 'Lately, I tend to think less at work and do my job almost mechanically'; Demerouti et al., [2003](#page-22-19)). Both burnout dimensions were reliably measured (*α*exhaustion=.72; *α*disengagement=.80) and answered on a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly disagree) to 4 (Strongly agree). **TABLE 1** Demographic variables for staff. | | Sex | | | | Years of experience | | | | | Age | | | | |---------------|------------|-------|-------|--------|---------------------|------------|------------|-----------|--------|-----------|-------------|-----------|--------| | | male

Abbreviation: *n* miss, number of participants missing. # Engagement in organizational outcomes Staff's engagement in organizational outcomes was assessed with three outcomes: organizational commitment, professional development and team morale. *Organizational commitment* was evaluated with a shortened version of the Organizational Commitment Questionnaire which assesses how committed participants are to the organization and the extent they do their best for their organization (Tetrick & Farkas, [1988](#page-24-21)). Five items (including 'I talk up this school to my friends as a great organization to work for') were answered. This scale demonstrated good reliability in Wave 1 (*α*=.80) and Wave 3 (*α*=.82). *Professional development* was assessed with six items created for the purpose of this research. Based on education literature, we assessed the extent to which respondents perceived that staff members sought and engaged in activities that developed their professional skills, with items such as: 'Staff are offered programs to develop their teaching knowledge and skills'. Staff answered these questions in Wave 1 (*α*=.88) and Wave 3 (*α*=.88). *Team morale* was assessed using the morale subscale of the school organizational health questionnaire (Hart et al., [2000](#page-22-20)). Participants responded to items assessing morale in their organization (e.g., 'Staff work with enthusiasm'). This scale showed good reliability in Wave 1 (*α*=.87) and Wave 3 (*α*=.86). # Covariates We included three demographic variables as covariates in our analyses: age, sex and teaching experience, all at Wave 3. Participants reported in what age category they fit (1=less than 35 years of age; 2=35–49 years of age; 3=more than 49 years of age) and their sex (1=Male; 2=Female; 3=Other). They also reported how many years of experience they had (1=less than 6 years; 2=6–10 years; 3=11–20 years; 4=more than 20 years). We also controlled for school climate and outcome variables at Wave 1, except for burnout which was only measured at Wave 3. # **Data analyses** Data used in this study has not been previously used in published articles. Data cleaning, missing data analysis, and descriptive statistics were completed using SPSS Version 26 while Mplus 8.3 was used to conduct multilevel model path analysis. Mplus analysis codes are available in the Data [S1](#page-25-5). To test whether identity leadership at Wave 1 impacted on staff well-being and commitment to work at Wave 3 via school climate (Wave 2), we used a set of hierarchical multilevel models built per dependent variable (which were centred at the school level). The multilevel models account for variance of leadership, school climate and outcome variables at both the individual (within) and the school (between) level. This within and between variance was examined with 'null models' (Model 0) that were run to get Muthen's ICCs (intra-class correlations, akin to the ICC1 but with slightly different estimators; Dyer et al., [2005](#page-22-21)). The ICCs estimate the variance at the between-level (Goldstein et al., [2002](#page-22-22)) and determine the extent to which the responses within schools are independent from each other (Hox, [2013\)](#page-22-23). Models then we built hierarchically while also examining the nested nature of the data for paths *a*, *b, c* and *c*′ in Figure [1](#page-4-0) with random intercepts for all models. This approach was necessary given that responses to identity leadership and school climate may also be clustered by (or nested within) schools. Following Model 0 (which tested the 'null model' to obtain the ICCs for all variables), Models 1 tested path *c* (Figure [1\)](#page-4-0). Specifically, Model 1a examined whether identity leadership at Wave 1 predicted the outcome variable at Wave 3 within individuals (i.e., at Level 1), while Model 1b tested whether the same pattern occurred at the school level, with school-averaged identity leadership predicting the outcome variables (i.e., at Level 2). We used Akaike's information criterion (AIC) and the difference test for log likelihood (Δ −2 LLR) to test whether adding the between-level associations significantly improved the fit of nested models above the within-level associations (e.g., from Model 1a to Model 1b).[1](#page-8-0) To investigate whether these relations held when controlling for confounding variables, Model 1c tested whether identity leadership at Wave 1 predicted better wellbeing and organizational engagement while controlling for age, years of experience, sex and the outcome at Wave 1, providing a test for [H1](#page-4-1). Importantly, we examine the relationship between initial levels of identity leadership and residuals (or changes) in mediator and outcome variables by accounting for their initial levels of the mediator and all outcomes but burnout (disengagement and exhaustion). Models 2 investigated path *b*, whether school climate at Wave 2 predicted the outcome variable within individuals (Model 2a) and between schools (Model 2b; with AIC and Δ −2 LLR used to compare these two nested models), even when including control variables (Model 2c). Models 3 tested path *a* and *b* simultaneously between individuals (Model 3a) and between schools (Model 3b; with Δ −2 LLR and AIC used to compare these models). The final model (Model 3c) tested [H2,](#page-4-2) the indirect path at the within and the school level while also adding all relevant covariates (age, sex and teaching experience), including school climate and the dependent variable at Wave 1. This enabled us to assess whether identity leadership is associated with *changes* in school climate and staff outcomes. Across all models, continuous within-school variables are group-centred. An indirect path is significant if it has *p<*.050 and the 95% confidence interval does not include 0. # **RESULTS** # **Data cleaning and descriptive analyses** Despite efforts to retain all participants across each wave of data collection, missing values analysis showed a missing rate across the three waves ranging from 34.6% to 56.4% for identity leadership, school climate, burnout (disengagement and exhaustion), stress, self-esteem, organizational commitment, team morale and professional development. For the demographic covariates (age, gender and teaching experience in 2020), the missing rate was between 41.4% and 68%. Little's MCAR test was also significant ( *p*<.001) which suggests that the data was not missing completely at random (not MCAR). Further exploration of the pattern of missing data suggests that missingness was related to other variables in the dataset (i.e., missing at random [MAR]; Newman, [2014](#page-23-18); Tabachnick & Fidell, [2013\)](#page-24-22). To retain as many cases as possible and obtain less biased and more powerful estimation of coefficients (Newman, [2014\)](#page-23-18), Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML with Estimation Maximization) in Mplus was used (Little & Rubin, [2002](#page-23-19)). FIML is a robust method for managing missing data, comparable to methods such as multiple imputation (Lee & Shi, [2021\)](#page-23-20).[2](#page-8-1) FIML uses all available data in the estimation process in a single step, including cases with missing values, producing a more efficient model and accurate parameter estimates than when missing data is ignored. Table [2](#page-9-0) shows the means and standard deviations of our main variables and Table [3](#page-10-0) shows these associations at Level 1 (the within level) and Level 2 (the between level). # **Hierarchical multilevel models** Model 0 was used to obtain the ICCs and calculate the design effects. As can be seen in Table [4](#page-12-0), across dependent variables, the ICCs ranged from .004 to .158, and the design effects were above two for all But not for Model 1c, as this was not a model nested in Model 1a/Model 1b. Our specific goals were two-fold. First, we examined the longitudinal impact of *identity leadership* on well-being and various types of organizational engagement. This question is critical to understand the relations and potential mechanism of group-based identity leadership, and hence, its influence. In line with [H1,](#page-4-1) staff members who perceived that their school leaders engaged in identity leadership reported less burnout engagement, burnout disengagement and stress, with a marginal association for self-esteem 2 years later while controlling for outcomes at Wave 1 (except for burnout outcomes) and demographic variables (teaching experience, age category and gender). These results were found at the within-level. Identity leadership also predicted higher levels of organizational engagement, as assessed by organizational commitment, team morale and professional development. This research provides clear evidence that supports the importance of placing the *group* at the heart of a leaders' ability to influence. Effective identity leaders shape both staff improved well-being and stronger engagement in organizational outcomes. Our results suggest that individual perceptions of identity leadership predict individual *changes* of well-being and organizational engagement (i.e., controlling for Wave 1: [H1](#page-4-1)) through changes *in school climate* (i.e., controlling for Wave 1: [H2](#page-4-2)). This was not the case for the between (or school) level. This appears to be the result of adding the outcome variable at Wave 1 at the between-level as a control variable (see Tables [S1–S7](#page-25-5) in the Data [S1](#page-25-5) for the models without controls) because overall, there is little change across time. It is also possible that the impact of leadership on building shared experiences among staff within the whole school may require longer time frames to be detected. Altogether, this research contributes to a better understanding of identity leadership and its potential consequences. Through the leadership's ability to represent, work towards and embed themselves in the relevant group, they can directly impact the way organizational staff experience their work environment, including policies, practices and values (Rousseau, [1988](#page-23-8); Schneider et al., [2013\)](#page-24-14). In turn, by changing the social environment of the group, identity leaders can support staff well-being and engagement. Our results open a potential path forward to reduce burnout and increase organizational engagement, namely by training leaders to become identity leaders. One such approach is the 5R program, which is designed to help leaders manage their group identities in the workplace to maximize social influence (Haslam et al., [2017](#page-22-24), [2021](#page-22-7)). In a randomized controlled trial, the program was shown to improve leaders' identity-related abilities (e.g., create a shared sense of 'us'; maintain team members' identification with the group; increase social support), improve team members' intrinsic motivation and confidence in their team's abilities, as well as lower burnout (Mertens et al., [2021](#page-23-23)). The current results suggests that identity leadership programs can be a catalyst for a stronger, cohesive group and its potential downstream consequences (well-being and engagement). # **Strengths and limitations** There are several strengths to this research. First, this research is theory-based, testing a series of psychological processes that had been hypothesized (Haslam et al., [2021\)](#page-22-7) but not tested. Second, this is one of few multiyear longitudinal examinations assessing the long-term associations between identity leadership, organizational climate and staff's well-being as well as engagement. Such investigation has not been done, particularly in schools. Additionally, by controlling for the mediator and the outcome variables at Wave 1, we were able to assess changes in these processes as a function of identity leadership. Third, we had a large sample size (over 6000 participants across 3 years) from 89 different schools. This enables us to assess the perspective of staff members across many schools. However, there are limitations to this research. While all longitudinal research has missing data, and even though missing data was treated appropriately and was robust to ways of treating missing data (Newman, [2014\)](#page-23-18), a smaller number of missing data would have been preferred. In addition, most of the variables were assessed via a survey answered by staff members. Thus, there is a possibility that the shared methods bias underly the statistical relationships that are observed. However, the multiyear nature of this research provides confidence that these variables are associated beyond the shared nature of data collection. There are also important and fruitful avenues for future research. While our sample size for people who *changed* organizations was insufficient to conduct a meaningful comparison (*n*=200), future research could examine how new staff who are introduced into schools with high versus low identity leadership experience well-being and engagement. Similarly, future research could investigate the degree to which staff within schools agree that their school has strong versus weak identity leadership agreement, and the extent to which such commonality in agreement impacts well-being and engagement. # **CONCLUSION** Our research illustrates that school leaders—and in particular school identity leaders—play an important role in shaping and strengthening the organizational climate of schools. By doing so, they are exercising their influence in promoting better well-being and organizational engagement This is particularly important in schools, where there are important flow-down effects for students and therefore the next generation.
